title: Antarctic Ozone Hole Is the Seventh Largest in 48 Years
paragraphs: NOAA and NASA have now published their annual reckoning of the Antarctic ozone hole, and the 2026 season emerges as notable but far from historic: the seventh largest in 48 years of observation. Averaged over the core window of September 7 to October 13, it covered about 25 million square kilometres, more than twice the area of the United States, and it reached its greatest extent on September 18, at roughly 27.1 million square kilometres, some 90 percent of the record set on September 9, 2000.

The agencies locate the cause in the atmosphere's own variability rather than in any resurgence of pollutants. A formidable polar vortex, kept intact by unusually sluggish planetary-scale waves through August and September, let the chemistry of ozone destruction run over a broader swathe of the stratosphere. Directly above the South Pole, total ozone dipped to 105 Dobson units on October 17, still above the 92 units logged in October 2006. The assessment draws on balloon-borne sondes, a ground-based Dobson spectrophotometer and a fleet of satellites, among them Aura, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and Suomi NPP.

The scientists take care not to let a large hole eclipse the larger story. By their estimate, had ozone-depleting substances persisted at their year-2000 peak, the hole would have spread one to two million square miles further, and stratospheric chlorine over Antarctica has already receded by about a third since its 1980s zenith, an achievement they credit to the Montreal Protocol of 1987. But the culprit molecules are stubbornly long-lived, so full recovery is pencilled in for the 2070s at the earliest, and in the meantime a single year's figures, whether flattering or alarming, say more about the weather than about the treaty's success.

questions.q: What does 'the atmosphere's own variability' refer to?
questions.a: Natural changes in weather and winds, not new pollution.

questions.q: Why is recovery not expected before the 2070s?
questions.a: The harmful molecules stay in the atmosphere for decades.

questions.q: What is the writer's view on judging the treaty by a single year?
questions.a: A single year says more about the weather than about the treaty's success.
